en: The sampaguita, the Philippine national flower, releases its strongest fragrance at night to attract pollinating hawkmoths.
The narra, our national tree, drops its small, winged seed pods during the dry season to help wind dispersal.
The Philippine eagle, our national bird, has specialized crest feathers that it can raise to look larger to predators.
Ifugao farmers build stone walls for the Banaue Rice Terraces to prevent soil erosion and retain water for rice paddies.
The South Sea pearl, our national gem, forms when a golden-lip oyster coats an irritant with layers of nacre.
The anahaw, our national leaf, has a large, fan-shaped structure that naturally sheds heavy rain to prevent tearing.
The Philippine carabao, our national animal, wallows in mud to cool its body because it lacks sweat glands.
Mayon Volcano in Albay forms a near-perfect cone because of alternating layers of hardened lava and loose volcanic ash.
The bangus, our national fish, has no teeth but uses specialized gill rakers to filter microscopic algae from water.
The waling-waling orchid grows high on tree branches in Mindanao to access better sunlight and avoid ground floods.
T'boli weavers sun-dry extracted abaca fibers to evaporate moisture, which increases the natural tensile strength of the weaving material.
The Puerto Princesa Underground River features stalactites formed by calcium carbonate deposits left behind as mineral-rich water drips.
